utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Bagic, you would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday morning at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Bagic.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the conclusion of the session I was --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was asking you about your contacts with government ministers other than Mr. Separovic in 1995 and you said you couldn't recall any specific contacts. And I'd like to ask you a similar question about any contacts you may have had with President Tudjman in 1995. Do you recall having any communication or contact with him at the time?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that I had any sort of contact with President Tudjman in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you -- did you know him then or not?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know him. Except, of course, through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him; and, if so, when was that?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met President Tudjman several times. Two times I met him personally. I do not remember the exact years. I believe that the first time it was before I was appointed deputy minister, and that was in 1997. The second meeting took place, I think, around 1999. And I think I was present at two meetings of the National Security Council, who were presided by President Tudjman. If I remember correctly, he was the president of this council. And I believe that these were meetings that were held in the period of the year 1998. It must have been in late spring when there was no minister at the Ministry of Justice. He wasn't performing his duty, in fact. The reason was that the previous minister had been relieved of his duty, and the newly appointed minister, at the time, Dr. Milan Ramljak was the Ambassador of the Republic of Croatia to Austria, so some time was needed for him to take care of his obligations as the Ambassador and assume his duty as the minister in the Ministry of Justice. So this is what I can say, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move on to the decree on the temporary takeover of property that you were asked questions about yesterday. And, in particular, you were asked whether you worked on this decree, on the drafting of the decree, and you said at page 26495: "Yes." And you explained: "Because I had previously taken part in the preparations and drafting of a law that had the exact same name." And you had explained that you started working on the law in June of 1995. My question is: When were you informed that a decree was to be enacted, and how were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date on which I was informed about that. As for the manner in which I was informed about it, it was certainly the way in which usually the minister of justice would inform me about this, when, at a meeting of the government or a government session, a decision of this kind would be made. He would then call the persons from the ministry who were competent or to whom he had assigned a certain task and tell them to do that. As the decree was adopted around the 31st of August, that was when the government session took place, and the decree was published in the Official Gazette, and it came into force on the 4th of September. If I'm not mistaken, then it must have been in the second half of August. But I really do not remember the specific details, and I cannot elaborate on the details from this point in time, as there are no written traces about this. There is not written information on the basis on which one could say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you recall now whether Mr. Separovic gave you any specific instructions or guide-lines regarding the decree, such as, for example, that it should have a 30-day time-limit?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that specifically. It seems to me that the instructions that were issued, in terms of drafting the decree, were not much different from the text of the bill, which we had already drafted. The text of this bill on temporary takeover and management of property, it had gone through the first reading in the parliament, and at the moment of the preparation and adoption of the decree, the emphasise was on the necessity to find a legal solution and adopt the regulation or a law that would regulate this issue of the temporary takeover and management of property as soon as possible, because at the time the Croatian parliament was not sitting and therefore the final bill could not be submitted to the Croatian parliament for the second reading. So this constitutional and legal possibility was to adopt a decree law and there was more discussion about this possibility, what the possibility was, and could anything specific be done about that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- I appreciate that you're trying to give detailed answers, but if could you try to focus specifically on the questions that I ask, because my time is limited. Thank you. Now, in we could go to Exhibit D422, which is the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property. Now, in your statement and in your testimony you described this law as having a twofold objective. First, to protect the property of Serbs who had left the area that had been occupied prior to Operation Storm; and, secondly, to house internally displaced persons and refugees, primarily from Bosnia. And you stated several times that the goal was to provide temporary housing for these displaced persons and refugees. And just to clarify those, those refugees and displaced persons, those were primarily Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said this a number of times. The law was not written so that it would distinguish between citizens on the basis of their ethnicity. However, the factual situation was such that particularly after the Operation Storm, quite a number of the citizens of Serbian ethnicity had left the Republic of Croatia and found residence in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On the other hand, the opposite process was also ongoing. Quite a large number of the citizens of Croatian ethnicity had come from the occupied territories, the territories of Republic of Croatia that were still occupied, to the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia. And, likewise, a large number of citizens of Croatian ethnicity from Bosnia-Herzegovina had come to Croatia. At the moment when the implementation began, most probably, there are various data about this that were not under my jurisdiction, mainly the citizens of Croatian ethnicity were accommodated in this property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at Article 2 of this law which is on this page in English and the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This law didn't only cover the property of Serbs who had left in connection with Operation Storm. It also covered property located anywhere in Croatia, belonging either to people who had left Croatia after the 17th of August, 1990, or people who were citizens of the FRY who were currently not using their property. And all of these three categories of property owners set out in Article 2, they were largely ethnic Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably were citizens of Serb ethnicity, but the first category that we talked more about yesterday were the citizens of Croatia, probably of Serbian ethnicity, as after these operations, they left the country. They were leaving it any way after the 17th of August, 1990, but, in particular, after Operations Flash and Storm. So these were Croatian citizens, most probably of Serb ethnicity, but certainly not only them who were leaving to the areas mentioned herein. And the third category which is maybe not particularly noted here because there was not a problem with their return to the Republic of Croatia, as Croatian citizens, were the citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who owned real estate in the Republic of Croatia - that is mentioned in paragraph 3 of Article 2 - and this was most often holiday homes which the citizens of the Federal Republic of Croatia owned or possessed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just in relation to the last part of your answer, you said they were probably most often holiday homes owned by, and it came out in translation as the citizens of the Federal Republic of Croatia, and I think that was supposed to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, maybe it was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine. And yesterday you were shown an UN document containing an analysis of the decree on temporary takeover. That was Exhibit D689. And that analysis concluded that the decree represents an act of discrimination. And you were asked whether you could find any provisions testifying to the existence of discrimination against citizens of Croatia with regard to their return to the country, and you replied at page 26526: "No, I cannot. This decree and the later law did not have that effect. It referred to the property of all citizens whose property was abandoned and not used personally by them." And I would just like to clarify that, because the decree and the law don't refer explicitly to ethnicity but the -- those who concluded that this law and decree were discriminatory were basing that conclusion on the fact that the groups of citizens whose property rights were affected by this law were largely ethnic Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness can complete her answer and then I will make a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually no comments are made but objections against questions. But if you prefer the witness to answer first, she has an opportunity to do so. Could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will, Your Honour. The law, as such, had the purpose and goal about which I talked on several occasions yesterday. That was primarily to protect the property, to which the law referred, and also to enable the accommodation of expelled persons, displaced persons, refugees, all those who were affected by the consequences of the war. These were also family members of Croatian defenders who were dead or had gone missing. These were persons who were now moving into these areas and who were supposed to enable with their revitalization. As for the implementation of the law, it was implemented depending on the situation in Croatia at the time, specifically in local areas, which had been occupied, and had now recently been liberated. So in the whole area of the Republic of Croatia, with the emphasise on the areas that had been occupied and which were now liberated. At the time in the Republic of Croatia, and not only in the Republic of Croatia, if you allow me to emphasise, but also in the neighbouring countries such as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, because of the consequences of war, there were great movements and migrations of the population. And in this situation people who were Croatian citizens, mostly of Serb ethnicity, were leaving Croatia and most often going to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Prior to Operation Storm they were also moving into the areas of the Republic of Croatia that were occupied at the time. And, on the other hand, within the Republic of Croatia, we had huge migrations of Croatian citizens of Croatian ethnicity who were moving -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We've now gone on for a page and you haven't answered my question. You might be getting to that, but in the interests of time I'm going move on to the next question because I don't have much time. But I would really like to ask you to focus on the specific question that I'm asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just in terms of the description of D689, just so that the record is clear, it was said that it's an UN document containing an analysis. Just so that it's clear, it's a Belgrade Helsinki committee analysis, which is then forwarded within the UN, just so that the record is clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson. And perhaps, Ms. Bagic, let's try, indeed, to focus on what apparently is the core of the question. The core of the question being that the comments may be inspired, although it may be difficult for you to say exactly what it is based on because it is comments by others, that the factual effect of legislation might not always be found in the wording of the legislation. If I adopt legislation on membership of sport organisations of people higher that 2 metres and 5 centimetres, no one will be surprised if the basketball Federation would say it was directed against them, although the word "basketball" may not even be mentioned in such legislation. That's, I think, as a matter of fact, the kind of issues we're discussing here that even if there's no clear reference to certain groups, that it is suggested by Ms. Gustafson that, nevertheless, the effect may be primarily on certain groups. I think that's what we're talking about, and there's no need to explain, again, what, as we find it already in your statement, the purpose of the legislation is because I take it that Ms. Gustafson is trying to take you to the effect of this legislation. Ms. Gustafson, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to page 4 in the English in this document and page 3 in the B/C/S to Article 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the provision that provides for the 90-day dead-line. And you were asked about this dead-line in your testimony yesterday, and this was in relation to the dead-line in the decree at page 26513, and you said: "At the moment when the decree was drafted, the intention was to resolve the relations as soon as possible. So by setting up this dead-line, we wanted to allow the owners to return as soon as possible and seek the restitution so that people could come into possession of their property as soon as possible." And you said "we wanted." By use of the word "we," in that phrase, "we wanted to allow the owners to return as soon as possible," who are you referring to? Are you referring to the Working Group that you were a part of that worked on drafting this law?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the Working Group, but I also had in mind the view of the government, that is to say, the view of the Croatian Parliament which adopted this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, in your view, the Croatian parliament took the same view as the Working Group because they passed the law, but you don't have any specific knowledge about what individual members of the parliament or the government, other than possibly Mr. Separovic, thought about this law, do you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at the government sessions when this topic was discussed. Therefore, I have no direct knowledge. The government adopted the bill unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you said that this view of the dead-line was the view of the Working Group, specifically what is the source of your information that causes you to conclude that that was the view of the Working Group about this dead-line?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already said that we attended meetings, that we were working on the wording of the law. We discussed the best possible dead-line to be included. So, therefore, I have this knowledge that originates from the period when we were working on this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you remember now, when Mr. Separovic informed you that this law -- that such a law was to be drafted, do you remember if he told you that there was to be dead-line for the return and repossession of the property? Can you recall that now?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to remember any details concerning specific discussions. In addition, the drafting of a bill or an enactment is a long-lasting process. At what particular moment within the Working Group or when it was that Mr. Separovic who was in charge of coordinating the work on drafting the law within the ministry, it was decided that some specific dead-line would be desirable, is nothing that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And yesterday you were also asked about the reason that the dead-line was changed from 30 days to 90 days, and you said -- and this is at 26533: "The dead-line was expanded from 30 days, as in decree, to 90 days, because, at least that's how it seems to me now from this point in time, because it turned out that it was not realistic that an owner could return within such a short time-span of 30 days and asked a restitution of his or her property. There were objective difficulties because there were great migrations of the population." Now, in that answer, you said that this was how it seems to you now from this point in time. And from that answer, I take it that you didn't know specifically at the time that the dead-line was changed, or you can't remember specifically what the reason was for the change in that dead-line, and you're just drawing a conclusion now about what you think that reason might have been. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Namely, this digression of mine had to do with the fact that I'm talking about the period that happened 15 years ago. It is difficult for one to remember all the details relating to the drafting of a document. However, I already said, and I will try to repeat this in brief, is the following. In the preparation of the document, and in making the amendments to it, along with representatives of the judiciary -- there is -- representatives of other ministries and institutions took part as well, and so did the representatives of the ministry of development. So when we were discussing the possible amendments to the wording, it was definitely obvious at the time that there were some obstacles and that the 30-day dead-line was not a realistic one, that it was to short. Therefore, in view of these difficulties, we sought to extend the dead-line to 90 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The draft law that you submitted to Mr. Separovic to take to the government to be debated by the parliament, did that contain a 30-day dead-line or a 90-day dead-line, or do you not remember?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we already had a 90-day dead-line. But I cannot confirm that with any certainty. Because there were no amendments to this law is something that makes me feel and think that already at that point the time-limit was 90 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when was -- when did you submit that law to Mr. Separovic to take to the government and the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot tell you the exact date. However, since the decree was adopted by the government on the 31st of August, and the Autumn sitting of parliament always starts after the 15th of September every year, we most probably prepared the final draft of the bill immediately after we did the original draft and gave it to Mr. Separovic or, rather, sent it to his office for him to submit this final draft of the law to the parliament of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in September 1995. Allow me just to -- to clarify. I'm referring to the final draft of the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of Property, since the bill had already been discussed and adopted by the parliament in July of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P475, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You were asked about the -- this further amendment to the Law on Temporary Takeover in January of 1996 where the 90-day dead-line was removed and the law instead stated that the issue of returning and possession and use would be regulated by the agreement on normalisation of relations between Croatia and the FRY. And you testified about the reason for removing that 90-day dead-line as follows, and this is at page 26534 and following: "During the implementation of this law, it turned out that whatever the dead-line was, that the dead-line was not realistic because there were such objective difficulties that one could not set any dead-line and then request the owner to request the restitution of his or her property. And perhaps the conclusions and impressions were wrong, so it was better to remove the dead-line and allow the owner to request restitution once he returns." Now, when you said that there were such objective difficulties that one could not set any dead-line and that perhaps the conclusions and impressions were wrong, one of the conclusions that was wrong was that these properties were abandoned, wasn't it? In fact, those properties weren't abandoned. There were thousands of Krajina Serbs who wanted to return to Croatia and repossess those properties, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. We are talking the property that, at the time, when the law was passed and being implemented, was abandoned. For that reason, we allowed for temporary possession of these properties. However, since the ownership was indisputable and this ownership was not affected in any way, there was an obligation to enable those who wanted to return to Croatia to establish or re-establish the ownership of these properties in Croatia. I think that we are talking here about two different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think so too. Were you involved in drafting this January amendment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interfere my learned colleague, but I have a remark on the transcript, as it refers to the translation of the Croatian word "posjed" which was translated as ownership. I don't believe this is a proper translation. So maybe if our interpreters could check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason to reconsider the declaration of the word which was pronounced by Mr. Mikulicic as "posjed"? Could I hear from the English and/or the French booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, the English translation supposedly of "posjed" could be either property or ownership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic -- and let me just check with the French booth first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, several comments were made by the booth about the translation of the word "posjed," so the Chamber is now aware that we should take specific care of that word and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but let me suggest something in order to be on the safe side. Could we ask the witness to define in legal terms, which is -- which is obviously very capable person to do so, to define the word posjed in a legal sense of word and the word "vlasnistvo," ownership, in a legal sense of word. So in order to avoid any misunderstanding on that terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would agree with you that we should invite the witness to explain what she meant when she used the word posjed. Now to suggest -- to explain another word which she hasn't used is perhaps something for cross-examination. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've had this issue come up with this word before, and I would just draw the Chamber's attention to page 18246 beginning at line 11 going through line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have no clear recollection of that. At the same time, even if at that time the matter was raised, then when a word may have different meanings then, of course, we should always ask the witness in what way he used that or she used that expression. Ms. Gustafson, I think it would save time if we do it right now and not wait until cross-examination because it might avoid malcommunication. So if you would invite the witness to explain what she mentioned when she -- what she meant when she used the word "posjed," that might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You heard the Judge, Ms. Bagic, if you could please, do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will and thank you for giving me an opportunity to give this explanation of what I mean when I wording -- using the word "posjed." The word "posjed" in our legal system means the ownership or the possession and practical use of an asset. I think that's the simplest explanation of the word posjed. It is one of the ownership powers in a broad sense which implies the right to dispose of the property. And "posjed" is only one of these rights and it involves practically the use of one's property or possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is an aspect of ownership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's one of the ownership aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, were you involved in drafting this January 1996 amendment to the Law on the Temporary Takeover? And if could you answer with a yes or no, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said -- again, when you were asked about the reasons for this amendment, you said: "It was better to remove the dead-line and allow the owner to request restitution once he returns." This amendment did not -- it removed the dead-line but it did not specifically allow the owner to request restitution once he returned. And my question is: Why, if, as you say now it would have been better to do that, did the Croatian authorities not just simply do that, just take the words "within 90 days" out of Article 11 and allow the owner to request restitution once he returned?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said yesterday that, at that time, the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were in the process of mutual communication relating to refugee issues. One of those segments was the anticipated and expected agreement on normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the FRY, which envisaged direct cooperation between competent authorities of the two states, as well as a joint commission that was supposed to exchange information and work on removing the obstacles relating to the return of citizens to their former places of residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We're talking here about the Croatian property rights of people who were born in Croatia and had lived virtually all of their lives in Croatia and may or may not have been residing in the FRY at the time. And it was not necessary to condition the Croatian property rights of Croatian Serbs on an agreement on normalisation with a foreign country, was it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem as far as sounds is concerned. I see that your microphones are switched on. Could you speak just a few words for a test of the sound, Ms. Bagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently these words were understood by the interpreters' booth. Let's slowly try to catch up again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, if you could repeat your answer from the beginning, because the translators couldn't hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Namely, later it turned out, and that was established by the constitutional court in its 1997 decision, that such prescribing the restitution of the property of Croatian citizens cannot be linked to the signing of the agreement, because those people were Croatian citizens and must enjoy the same rights as all the other Croatian citizens. Therefore, this provision was quashed by the constitutional court. However, when this amendment was made and the restitution was governed in a certain way, the intention was to enable these people, our citizens who had abandoned their property but were wishing to return, to do so at the time that they deemed the most appropriate with regard to their wishes and that it wouldn't be advisable to impose any deadlines.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were you given instructions when this amendment was drafted to condition the property rights of these Croatian citizens on a normalisation agreement with Yugoslavia; and, if so, who gave you these instructions?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive any instructions that would condition the restitution on the signing of this agreement on normalisation of relations. They were still the owners. Therefore, the issue was to enable them to take possession of their property and to allow them to use it practically in the Republic of Croatia. This was probably an indication that there was a certain draft of this agreement being prepared, and that, for that reason, it would be advisable to change the dead-line for restitution. If you allow me, I would just like to add the following: We were faced with a situation when there was intensive communication between the Ministry on the one side, while, at the same time, the process of finding accommodation and the process of return of refugees and IDP was subject of very intense communication and talks with representatives of the international community. Very often, particularly at that time, I think that there was some mixup between property right and the rights to restitution and practical use. In order to avoid such erroneous interpretations, we believed that it was better not to link restitution to any dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't believe you've answered my question, so I'm going to try to ask it more specifically. Did you receive any instructions to make the issue of returning and possession and use of property conditional on the signing of an agreement on normalisation of relations with the FRY; and, if so, who gave you those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going object. I believe the first sentence of the last answer, answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. The focus was on ownership, and I think we got sidetracked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the follow-up of the answer, it is unclear whether it is a real answer to the question. So the question simple is you get rid of the time-limit; it's apparently replaced by another condition, that is, an agreement between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the normalisation of the relations. Now, did you receive from anyone instruction or guidance to say, Well, the 90 days should be replaced by the condition of the agreement between Croatia and the Federal Republic. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Since the question was relating to ownership, that's why I gave my answer in the way I did. As far as restitution is concerned, as people who work in -- both in the ministry and on the amendment to this law probably from the government and competent ministries we received information that the restitution issue would be governed and resolved by the agreement and that would affect particularly Article 11, paragraph 2 of the Law on Takeover and Management of the property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's a long, but this reference to such an agreement was adopted in the draft on the instructions of the government. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would try to make your answers as short and as clear as possible, that would be appreciated. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Bagic, this -- the law as amended here did not contain any mechanisms for Krajina Serbs to repossess their property that had been taken over. And we looked yesterday at the agreement on normalisation, which is Exhibit D412, that came into effect some eight months after this amendment, and it also didn't provide any mechanisms to allow Krajina Serbs to repossess their property. And the first time such mechanisms were put in place was under the June 1998 return programme that you were shown yesterday, and, in particular, the provisions under point 9 of that programme. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, because as for the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of Property, regardless of the amendment to Article 11, paragraph 2, and the time-limit that we talked about, there was still a provision that if an owner should return and request the repossession of property that this would be quashed and the property would be returned to the owner.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Where is that provision?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That provision is linked with Article 8, I believe, and Article 11 of the Law on the Temporary Takeover.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, we've got the Article 11 here. It doesn't provide any mechanisms for Krajina Serbs to repossess their property, does it? And if we could also go back to D422 and Article 8 of that law so you could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's at page 3 of the English, and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it will be easier for the witness to follow the examination by having a hard copy of the -- of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Ms. Gustafson has no objection to providing the witness with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, not at all, if Mr. Mikulicic has a spare one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your assistance is appreciated, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] The provision of Article 11, paragraph 2 of the law is still there, and it says --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry to interrupt you. Article 11, as we just saw, was replaced by the amendment in January of 1996. So the Article 11 you're looking at now no longer existed as of January 1996.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partly right, because in Article 11, paragraph 1, it was the one that was changed. Then it says that the issue of returning the property for possession and use, but now I don't see it anymore -- or now this was quashed as part of the agreement of -- on normalisation between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But paragraph 2 remained there. It hasn't been changed, and it says against it's decision by which the commission quashed the decision under Article 5 of this law, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that he cannot interpret this at that speed. We don't have a hard copy. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slowly read the portion you referred to because the interpreters were not able to follow you due to the speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. So the provision remained, which reads: "Against the decision by which the commission quashed the decision under Article 5 of this law, the owner of the property, the person to whom this property was given for use, the ombudsman can file an appeal with the Ministry of Justice or to the ombudsman."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's a provision that allows certain persons to dispute a ruling that gives away a property for possession and use under Article 5, but there was no provision allowing an owner to request repossession of their property under the amended 1996 law, was there?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Namely, perhaps the provision in paragraph 1 was not phrased in the best possible way. However, what really existed and what was implemented in practice, and it has to do with the entirety of this law, was that the owner could always, once he returned, request the repossession of his property, because that was his basic right as the owner.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how would he do that without any provision in this law providing a mechanism to do so?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could do it because, if he really was the owner, according to the Law on Basic Property Law, and, later on, it was another law, according to which he could request the Housing Commission to allow him to repossess the property, and it was always his right to file a complaint with the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly what that law is and exactly what provision you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the Law on Basic Property Relations which the Republic of Croatia took over after the break-up of Yugoslavia, and we are talking about the Law on Ownership and other legal affairs which came into force on the 1st of January, 1997. And I think that in the provisions in Article 160 and 162 it reads that an owner may ask for protection, that is to say, to ask for restitution or repossession of his property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those laws didn't make any specific reference to the Law on Temporary Takeover in those provisions, did they?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are no references because these are basic laws, and the Law on the Temporary Takeover was a special law which regulated the status of property which had been abandoned at a certain point in time. Let me not repeat everything else that we have been talking about until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware of any case where a Krajina Serb, between the time of this amendment in January 1996 and the time that the mechanisms for repossession were instituted in 1998, are you aware of any case where a Krajina Serb was able to successfully repossess their taken-over property?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't really my duty. This was part of the competence of other ministries, so I cannot give you this information. What I do know is that this process of repossession was implemented in accordance with the procedures provided by this law, and the relevant bodies were in charge of that. And, of course, if someone filed a complaint with a court, then court proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you are not aware of any case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have such information at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, again, going back to what you said yesterday about the reason for the deadlines in the temporary takeover law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could I ask a few questions to clarify. This law on the temporary taking over, you said, was a special law. Would this mean that as long as the property was abandoned that that law would apply and not the basic law? Was it considered the lex specialis which would derogate from the application of a general law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this law was a special law in the sense that it regulated the issue of abandoned property and the possession of this property and, in that sense, the issue of possessing this property and the temporary use of it, it was a special law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which doesn't answer my question yet. Is whether you could invoke if the property was abandoned, whether you could invoke the basic legislation on ownership or not, the legislation you just referred. Would that apply in a court, or would the court say, No, you should make your application under the Law of the Temporary Takeover because it's abandoned property and that is what that lex specialis is meant for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The owner could refer to the basic law on property relations and request eviction. However, the courts could also establish the right of the owner to repossess the property. However, in practice, in courts, this law was also applied in court proceedings when eviction was requested on the basis of the law on property, the courts would decide that -- to put it simply, the decision would not be implemented as long as the temporary user was not provided with appropriate accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seem to be two different issues. The first one is whether the eviction would be effective if no accommodation has been found for the temporary user of that property, which is not the same issue. I think we see that in the decision -- the judgements of the European Court on Human Rights which you referred to. Is my recollection right, that the lex specialis issue played a role in the proceedings in Strasbourg, that applicants were sometimes confronted with inapplicability of certain laws because special laws, ruling on these matters, would apply and not the laws they invoked? I have to re-read it, but perhaps it's -- you have a clear recollection on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Namely, the issue of repossession of property and the accommodation of expelled persons and refugees, after the decree and the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of Property, with its amendment, was later regulated by the Programme for the Return of Expelled Persons, Refugees, and Displaced Persons from 1998, which is also referred to in the Law on the Termination of Validity of the Law on Temporary Takeover and Management of Property. And I mentioned this because the Programme for the Return of Expelled Persons, Displaced Persons, and Refugees and the Law on the Invalidation of the Law on Temporary Takeover included a decision to make the housing commissions in charge of enabling the repossession of property and, as well, the municipal courts, and that in these proceedings, which would be summary proceedings, the provisions on -- the provisions of the general administrative law would then be applied. Later on and some decisions of the European Court of Human Rights also referred to this, it was regulated by the Law on Areas of Special State Care, and the commission which was competent was taken over by the ministry of development and reconstruction. And the state attorney's office of the Republic of Croatia was now in charge of court proceedings. I am mentioning this because during this process of repossession and allocating accommodation to refugees and displaced persons, the competence changed. They were shifted from one body to another. So with the shift of the competence, some bodies were declared competent or not, or they would send this to another body, most often the housing commission. And in the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights in some of the decisions not all of them, it is noted that this procedure of resolving the repossession lasted too long and that the length of time during which the issue was being resolved actually violated the rights of the applicant. And the European Court of Human Rights did not question the competence and the authority of the bodies who were to decide about this, but they referred to the length of time in some of the cases which ended up before the European Court of Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree that they do not only consider the length of time but also the effective access to court proceedings in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in that sense, considering the duration of the proceedings, it was not a very effective manner to settle this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not an effective manner of settling matters, but the access to courts was ineffective which was resulted in the Radanovic case of a violation of Article 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights, isn't it? It's not just a matter of time. It's not just an effective settlement, but it is access to courts which turns out to be ineffective, perhaps for the reasons you explained, that the competence changed again and again; conditions changed several times. The issue, apparently, is the following, Ms. Bagic. You're telling us that out of an abundance of caution you wanted to return these people within 30 days and if that was unrealistic then in 90 days and then that a system should be there to have them all returned. What we find in these decisions is that those who are following all the court and bureaucratic rules, apart from those who got lost in some of the other cases, that, after six years, it took them six years to get their property -- the use of their property back. That's -- that's apparently what keeps you and Ms. Gustafson apart. She wants to draw your attention to the elements I just mentioned; whereas, you are emphasizing how -- how caring the legal system was for those who wanted to return. Would you -- if I try to explain what keeps you apart, would have you any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me to clarify what I was just talking about. The system was envisaged in such a way, and so was it written, that relatively quickly repossession of property should be enabled. However, what we are talking about now, and that's the application of this system, it cannot be excluded that it wasn't always effective. It certainly wasn't effective in some individual cases. That was one of the reasons why these laws were changed, why the programme was adopted, why the programme itself was later changed. These were reactions to its imperfections and to what turned out to be inapplicable in practice. Of course, that is why cases cannot be excluded in which the proceedings really lasted very long. From the point of view of the person who was asking for the repossession of property, it was certainly too long; and that was why, in some cases, the European Court did establish that there was a violation or infringement that, in particular cases, considering the circumstances of that case, the mechanisms which the owner had at his disposal were not efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now one final matter: Abolishing the 90 days and replacing it by an agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You emphasised several times that the matter was -- the legislation was not intended for Serbs or for whatever ethnic group. What about citizens which had no relation with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. How would this making them dependant between Croatia and a state with which they had nothing to do would that not even be a -- another obstacle? Why only an agreement with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and not Bosnia-Herzegovina, not Italy, not ... Could you explain why such an agreement on which various owners may have had no influence whatsoever, would, nevertheless, be the condition for repossession of their property.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not the condition for returning the property for repossession because the owners could always come back and request to repossess their property. And why only with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Because the Republic of Croatia had been attacked. There was an aggression against the Republic of Croatia by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as part of the former Yugoslavia; and it was important, at that time, immediately after the war, to normalise the relations. And the prospect was only that an agreement like that could be concluded with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is the best explanation I can give as to whether there was only an agreement of this kind envisaged with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which introduces another matter. Is it true that, in order to return, that those who owned property in Croatia, they were dependant on the conclusion of such an agreement? At least they were not free to return. And I'm talking about Serbs living in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Even though the agreement was not concluded, at that period they could still return, if the wanted to, being Croatian citizens. And they could exercise all their rights just as all the other Croatian citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Court has heard evidence on thoughts about whether a mass return could be allowed or not. Could you -- do you have any views, or do you have any knowledge on such views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no direct information about that, because I did not work directly on the return of expelled persons, displaced persons, and refugees. I did work on drafting these documents, especially the decree and the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of certain property. But as for the procedures that had to do with return, I only have some indirect knowledge about this, as someone who did take part in certain coordinations that had to do with all the issues relating to the returning of expelled persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us about your indirect knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not incorrect knowledge, it is indirect knowledge. Because the issues relating to the return of expelled persons, displaced persons, and refugees were issues that were discussed at working meetings or coordination meetings of the government. Even after the year 2000, there was a special coordination that was founded for areas of special state care, when all the conditions and procedures relating to the return of expelled persons and refugees were discussed. And I already said there were attempts to remove the difficulties that were noted on the ground, in connection with the application of the law or the -- the existing practice. The result of the all this, after the law and special after the decision of the constitutional court, was also the adoption of a document which is believed to be an operational document which is binding legally and that was the Programme for the Return of Expelled Persons, Displaced Persons, and Refugees. And I believe that it provided in more detail various situations relating to the return of expelled persons, displaced persons, and refugees, so I refer to this document. And the information I have about what this document contains in connection with, on the one hand, simplification and, other hand, more detailed provision of the conditions under which the expellees and refugees were to return to Croatian and repossess their property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do I understand that as long as these programmes and plans were developed that there was no free return for everyone who wished to return, because you so much emphasised in the beginning that your primary aim was to get everyone back who wished to go back but that they were dependant on finalising these programmes, projects, Working Groups, whatever they were, agreements. I'm trying to get to the core of what apparently is put to you by Ms. Gustafson and by the Prosecution and what the Chamber would like to get a better insight in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. It is not the issue that persons were not allowed or were not given an opportunity to return. The situation was such that, despite the adopted regulations and the efforts to implement them, it turned out that there were still objective difficulties in the process of their implementation. Therefore, it was the duty of the state to react and change such procedures and regulations, to endeavour to improve them, to make them as transparent as possible, because if there were indications that in the implementation of these regulations they do not produce the effects that were desired, then procedures should be simplified and be more accessible to those to whom they referred. That was the intention of these changes and this whole evolution that took place with regard to the legal framework for the return of expelled persons, displaced persons, and refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We will have a break. Ms. Gustafson, apologies on intervening, but sometimes it's better to hear the evidence in the context of what is raised by a party at that very moment. We'll resume at 11.00 after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, just before the break, in answer to a question from His Honour Judge Orie, you explained that you did not work directly on issues of return and you had no direct information about whether or not a mass return of Serbs would be permitted. And just to follow up on that, I'd like to ask you, more specifically, in 1995, is it right that did you not have a role in establishing or implementing Croatia's policies on the return of Serbs to Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a role in creating the policy, in terms of adopting political decisions. I also don't think that this is not to do with permitting or not permitting the return, but, rather, the manner in which that would be made possible, as well as about the procedures for effecting the return, of course, in compliance with the regulations of the Republic of Croatia. As a lawyer and an expert who carried out different duties within the Ministry of Justice, I did take part in drafting the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In 1995, did you take part in drafting any regulations regarding the return of Serbs to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which regulations you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't have any in mind. As far as I'm aware, there aren't any. But you said you took part in drafting different -- drafting regulations. I'm asking you if you worked on drafting any regulations regarding the return of Serbs to Croatia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did take part in drafting the law and the decree, that is to say, the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Management of certain properties, which, inter alia, referred to the Croatian citizens of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We know you took part in drafting that law. Did you take part in drafting any other regulations regarding the return of Serbs to Croatia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any such regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the Chamber has heard evidence of members of the top Croatian leadership, including President Tudjman, Mr. Sarinic, Mr. Jarnjak, discussing these issues, in particular, the issues you were referring to, the manner in which Serbs would return, procedures for effecting the return, and the timing of such return, as well as whether or not there would be a mass return. Do you know anything about those discussions or the decisions of the leadership about those matters in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So when you referred to objective difficulties to return in the context of the deadlines in the property and the temporary takeover of property law, you aren't really in a position to say, are you, to what extent the decisions taken by the leadership about the manner and timing of the return of Serbs affected the ability of Serbs to return to Croatia, are you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just so I understand you, you're saying it's correct that you are not in a position to talk about those matters.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, going back to the -- the deadlines in the decree and the Law on the Temporary Takeover of Property, the reason you gave for the extension of the dead-line from 30 to 90 days and then its removal was that the deadlines turned out to be unrealistic. And the Chamber has also heard evidence that the deadlines under the temporary takeover decree and law were extended and then lifted under considerable pressure from members of the international community, including, in particular, the US and the EU. Do you have any specific information about international pressure being put on Croatia, in relation to these deadlines at this time, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any specific information about the pressure from the international community, both with regard to the implementation of the law itself and the deadlines.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, you testified yesterday that the reason for the deadlines in the temporary takeover law was that you wanted to allow the owners to return as soon as possible and seek their restitution, and you explained that was the view of the Working Group. Now, in fact, whatever the view of the Working Group was, the real reason for these deadlines and other limitations on the ability of Serbs to repossess their properties was that the Croatian leadership wanted to permanently resettle Croats into Serb-owned houses and prevent the return of those Serbs to Croatia. Do you have anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that, because I don't have any knowledge about that. The purpose and the aim of the regulations in the way that they were set up was to enable the owners to repossess their property wherever it was located in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And to clarify, that was the purpose, as far as you were aware and as far as the Working Group was aware; is that right? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about what I know, and I know what the task of the Working Group was. I know what the regulations were. And I also know how they were implemented, in practice, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to D1823, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bagic, this is the 31st of August closed session of the government, the minutes that were shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 11 in the English and page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is Mr. Separovic speaking here. And at the top of the page in the B/C/S and near the bottom of the page, beginning in the second paragraph of his speech, you can see he says: "I absolutely support the law. The decree is a bit legally and constitutionally questionable, but since we know for sure that the law will be passed, then this possible unconstitutionality, constitutionality will be dismissed. I propose that the Article 11 actually be altered considerably in agreement with the vice-president; it should not mention the ownership and how to acquire ownership, but, rather, to have one provision saying that this issue is to be resolved by a separate regulation ..." And then in the next paragraph he says: "We can have objections here that in this way we are promoting nationalisation, that there is property owned by the Republic, that we are carrying out nationalisation; we could face the accusations, as our constitution does not allow it. And in this other case, if we transfer the [sic] ownership right onto those persons, then we have here an adverse possession, then we have a case of acquiring ownership through an institute of adverse possession, and in that case we have this basic time-limit of 20 years. This is too long for us to wait. That is why I would opt for the proposal set down by the vice-president, Misetic ... to shelf this matter for the time being. This issue of regulation of the ownership right; and that the dead-line for filing the request for repossession ... be set on 30 days from the day the law comes into effect ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could now move to page 14 in the English and page 26 in the B/C/S, starting at the bottom of the page in the English and near the top of the page in the B/C/S. If we could move down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is Mr. Bosiljko Misetic speaking now. And he says -- it's about three lines down in the B/C/S: "This is one thing and the government should define this precisely and say if they support this idea that it is given away for use, provided that a lex specialis is to eventually regulate this issue of ownership or are we to grant them ownership right away? My personal opinion" --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please. "My personal opinion is that it is more prudent in a political sense of the word, if we, at this particular moment, give it away for use only."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom of this page in the English and the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Simunovic is speaking. And beginning at the second sentence of his speech, he says: "When we look from the point of view of the foreign policy, there will be certain expenses, as well as a considerable coercion. It specifically applies to Article 11; I am referring to Article 11 in particular and to what Mr. Prus, Separovic, and Pavlovic say here, i.e., the principle of sanctity and inviability of the property, as when we speak of the coercion, the pressure will be the hardest when it comes to the use of the term property." And then the next page in English: "Using the property is one thing, as the western world is highly rational. They will accept the preservation of the capital, preservation of the resources. But the infringement on other people's property is something that contravenes the principles of the constitution of the western societies, ergo, I am entirely for the variant that tends to treat the question of an aspect of foreign policy of using rather than to infringe on the property be it only provisional in round one." And, finally, if we could go to page 19 of the English and page 33 of the B/C/S. And this is Prime Minister Valentic speaking. And it's at the at the top of the page in B/C/S and near the bottom of the page in English, starting at the second sentence of the last paragraph: "Secondly, I propose that the acquisition of ownership be defined by a separate law. We have neither time nor possibility now, nor is it necessary that we encounter all those political hazards and minefields; therefore, we have time to calmly regulate the issue of ownership in a separate law. I suggest that this be a second position. The only problem I see as disputable and a dangerous one is Article 11 which explicitly says that if, within a certain dead-line, one does not register, it shall then become the state ownership. And I think that it can be politically very dangerous for us. Therefore, I suggest that, once again, we consider here and in the inner cabinet tomorrow morning, if necessary, together with the Ministry of Justice, how to define it, that it still remains a sequestration. "If we infringe the ownership, we are faced with the danger to suffer an indefensible attack, not to mention to which extent the ownership is sacred in the west and how much we should advocate for the private ownership and, as a state, we have the possibility of management. People who enter must have the security of usage, so we shall see how to resolve the issue of ownership. And even if we could pass the ownership to them, we would not do that, due to the reasons mentioned by the Deputy Prime Minister Misetic. As might be expected, there will be cases of reselling, misuse, so it will be necessary to establish the criteria." Now, you explained today that you worked on the -- drafting the property law decree that was submitted to the government and discussed at this session. And yesterday in your evidence you said - and this is at page 26505: "When a law or a decree were being drafted, we never discussed seizure of ownership or the right to property in any way whatsoever." Now, is it not the case that as was discussed here and as specifically mentioned by the prime minister, that the decree that was presented to the government and that they discussed at this session actually did provide for a transfer of ownership of property to the state under Article 11 but the participants decided that that would not be wise. Is that right, that the original decree that was presented to the -- draft decree that was presented to the government provided for an outright transfer of ownership to the state.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that one of the options was this one, in view of the fact that before there were plenty of cases of swapping or sale of the property. However, eventually, the version that all the experts advocated was adopted, and therefore it was decided not to infringe upon the right to ownership as an inalienable right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, as we can see from the discussion, that's what the government decided here. But the draft of the decree that you and the Working Group presented to Mr. Separovic to discuss at the government did contain a provision for the transfer of ownership under Article 11. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a number of experts took part in this. The decree with contents like this usually have some alternatives. It is possible that one of the alternatives was that with the fact that we also observed that there are many dangers implied in such a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you saw in this discussion, in particular, the comments of the prime minister and Mr. Simunovic that this provision for the outright transfer of ownership would be politically dangerous and they referred to the views of western nations. Were you involved in any discussions about the political considerations that might affect the wording of these -- this decree or the law such as those mentioned by the prime minister and President Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not participate in any political discussions. I only participated in expert discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could now go to 65 ter 3D00959.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Bagic, these are the minutes of the -- an open session of the government held also on the 31st of August, 1995, apparently immediately after the closed session that we just looked at, and this is the session where the decree is, in fact, adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 17 in the English and page 22 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is part of a speech by Mr. Cedomir Pavlovic. And Mr. Pavlovic was an ethnic Serb and the only ethnic Serb member of the government at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please. Whether it's right whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I did not know that I was expected to provide an answer. I suppose that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you know that or do you suppose it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. I do not know that Mr. Pavlovic was the only representative of the Serbian ethnic group in the Government of Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you are aware that he was a -- he is an ethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take that in account, but I believe that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could look at the last full paragraph in the B/C/S. And this is it the fourth paragraph down in the English, beginning with the words: "If I might ..." And Mr. Pavlovic says -- and they're discussing the decree now in open session: "If I might be permitted to underline a small dilemma, this is to do with deadlines, what the deadlines refer to. I understand that the deadlines refer to what is established, 30 or 45 days in the submission of the intent by citizens of the Republic of Croatia to return to their property and use that property. It says 'when they return.' I am not sure that this will be sufficient for proper procedure in accordance with humanitarian regulations, because, from my experience, from the discussion at the last session of the government, I do not know whether we have ultimately determined the procedure of how those who wished to return are to do so."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He goes on: "In fact, from the information which I have from the press where it is said, I cannot be 100 per cent sure of this, but there is an good proportion of our citizens who have left the now liberated areas, who have registered at our office in Belgrade and who would like to return to our and their homeland through humanitarian organisations. I mean, I shall be brief, that one has to determine a return procedure, who they are to be registered with, who will do the processing in the Republic of Croatia so that they can claim their right under Article 10 of this decree, so that they can return, because essentially, then, the return procedure, so they would be able to return, because otherwise it would happen that they want to return but have not returned" --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English. "... within a period of 30 days or whatever dead-line is decided. And therefore the actual act of returning would be qualified for them as it is in the decree, and so they have not come to their homeland and have not been able to regain their property."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you gave evidence that it became apparent at some stage that the 30-day dead-line was not realistic. Did you know that Mr. Pavlovic actually expressed his concern to the government that the deadlines in the decree, coupled with the fact that there were no procedures for Serbs to return, would mean that Serbs who wanted to return to Croatia to repossess their property within the dead-line would not be able to do this and that this posed a dilemma?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could just ask for a context of Mr. Pavlovic's position given that it says that he has expressed concern. I noted that the first two paragraphs of Mr. Pavlovic's position weren't presented to the witness. This is at page 17 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, he started by saying he wanted to point to a dilemma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not how he started, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the passage that I read, that's how he started: "If I might be permitted to underline a small dilemma. It's a dilemma, concern; I don't care." We can take out the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, is there any specific portion you would like to suggest to Ms. Gustafson then she can decide whether or not to give this context. If not, of course, although have you not examined the witness, I would grant an opportunity to provide the context you consider the most relevant, if Ms. Gustafson would not follow any of your suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right at the beginning of his presentation under his name, the first full paragraph, and the sentence -- the first sentence of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if would you read them and make up your mind whether or not you provide the context or leave it, rather, to Mr. Misetic at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't think it answers the context, but I'm happy to read it out just to save time. In that sentence, he says: "It is difficult not to agree that this decree needs to be issued for the sake of the comprehensive protection of property in the state of Croatia and that it must be supported in any event because of, above all, it is placed beneath the supervision and protection of the state organs just as is put in the decree."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Bagic, my question was about the dilemma Mr. Pavlovic raised in respect of the dead-line and the fact that the 30-day dead-line coupled with the fact that there were no procedures for return of Serbs at the time meant that -- that Serbs would -- who wanted to return within the dead-line to repossess their property would not be able to do so. Were you aware that this was pointed out to the government by a government member at the time the decree was passed?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could just stay on page 18 of the English and go to page 24 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the prime minister speaking now. At the end of the second paragraph and the second half of that paragraph, he says: "I think that here for the sake of the public it is necessary to stress that if anyone received that basic draft of the decree and law that Article 11 should be struck out, where in one draft it talked about possible separate possibilities of transfer to ownership, because we have concluded that it is necessary to define and resolve that very sensitive question of ownership by a completely new law." Now, again, here he is referring to the fact that the draft of the decree was first presented to the government provided for a transfer of ownership, right?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA BAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that the text of the decree in one of the first versions included something like that or that it included certain options.
